rows.query: Up to what value can a Ministry buy directly on GeM from any available supplier, without comparing sellers?
rows.answer:
The maximum value a Ministry can buy directly on GeM from any available supplier without comparing sellers is up to Rs. 50,000/-, provided the supplier meets the requisite quality, specification, and delivery period [ncs_manual_2025:4.6.3]. There is an exception for automobiles, where direct procurement is permitted without any ceiling limit [ncs_manual_2025:4.6.3]. 

For vendor screening and bid scoring in such scenarios, the rules state that suppliers' credentials on GeM are certified by GeM SPV, and the procuring authorities will certify the reasonability of rates [goods_manual_2024:4.17.2]. The tools for online bidding and reverse auction on GeM are available for procurements up to Rs. 10,00,000/-, and the evaluation process involves comparing bids and ensuring compliance with quality and delivery requirements [gem_gtc_4_0:C4]. 

The rules do not mention any specific exceptions or special cases for vendor screening or bid scoring in direct procurement scenarios, except for the automobile exception [ncs_manual_2025:4.6.3].

args.query: maximum value a Ministry can buy directly on GeM without comparing sellers

rows.query: We need to buy items worth Rs 6 lakh that are available on GeM. How must the seller be chosen?
rows.answer: The process for selecting a seller on GeM for items worth Rs 6 lakh involves choosing the GeM Seller with the lowest price among at least three different manufacturers, provided they meet the quality, specification, and delivery period requirements [goods_manual_2024:4.17.2]. This applies to procurements above Rs.50,000/- and up to Rs.10,00,000/- [gfr_2017:R149]. The procurement process on GeM is end-to-end, from placing supply orders to payment to suppliers, ensuring transparency and efficiency [ncs_manual_2025:4.6.3]. The procuring authorities must also certify the reasonability of rates [gem_gtc_4_0:C4].

args.query: process and guidelines for selecting a seller on GeM for items worth Rs 6 lakh

rows.query: For a GeM purchase above Rs 10 lakh, is it enough to pick the cheapest listed seller?
rows.answer: For a GeM purchase above Rs 10 lakh, it is not enough to pick the cheapest listed seller. According to Rule 149 of GFR 2017, purchases above Rs 10,00,000 must be made through the supplier with the lowest price after mandatorily obtaining bids using online bidding or reverse auction tools on GeM [gem_gtc_4_0:C4]. Additionally, the procurement process requires that the buyer ensures the selected seller meets the necessary quality, specification, and delivery period criteria [goods_manual_2024:4.17.2]. The cheapest seller may not always meet these requirements, and the buyer must evaluate all bids thoroughly [gem_gtc_4_0:C4].

rows.query: An item is not available on GeM. Up to what value can we purchase it without inviting quotations, and what is needed?
rows.answer:
The maximum value threshold for purchasing an item without inviting quotations when it is not available on GeM is Rs. 50,000/- for general procurements [goods_manual_2024:4.12], and for Scientific Ministries/Departments, it is enhanced to Rs. 1,00,000/- for scientific equipment and computers [goods_manual_2024:4.12]. For procurements above Rs. 50,000/- and up to Rs. 5,00,000/-, a Local Purchase Committee is required [goods_manual_2024:4.13]. 

To make such a purchase, the necessary documentation includes a "GeM Availability Report and Past Transaction Summary" (GeMAR&PTS) with a unique ID generated on the GeM portal [goods_manual_2024:4.17.2]. Additionally, a certificate from the competent authority confirming the purchase is reasonable and meets the required specifications is needed [gfr_2017:R154].

args.query: maximum value threshold for purchasing an item without inviting quotations when it is not available on GeM and necessary documentation or procedures required for such a purchase

rows.query: Is the limit for purchase without quotation different for scientific departments such as DRDO or ICAR?
rows.answer: The limit for purchase without quotation for scientific departments such as DRDO or ICAR is higher than the general limit of Rs. 50,000, with the limit for scientific equipment and computers enhanced to Rs. 1,00,000 for each case [goods_manual_2024:4.12]. Additionally, for procurement outside GeM, scientific ministries/departments can purchase goods up to Rs. 2,00,000 on each occasion [gfr_2017:R154].

args.query: Is the limit for purchase without quotation different for scientific departments such as DRDO or ICAR?

rows.query: How are goods worth around Rs 3 lakh bought when they are not on GeM?
rows.answer: Goods worth around Rs 3 lakh that are not available on GeM can be procured through the recommendations of a Local Purchase Committee [gfr_2017:R155]. This committee is constituted by the Head of the Department and is responsible for ensuring the goods meet the required specifications and are priced reasonably [gfr_2017:R155]. Additionally, a "GeM Availability Report and Past Transaction Summary" (GeMAR&PTS) must be generated and submitted as a prerequisite for such procurement [goods_manual_2024:4.17.2].

args.query: How are goods worth around Rs 3 lakh bought when they are not on GeM?

rows.query: From what estimated value must goods be procured through an advertised tender enquiry?
rows.answer: The estimated value of goods that must be procured through an advertised tender enquiry is Rs. 1,00,00,000/- (Rupees one crore) and above for Scientific Ministries/Departments/Organizations of Government of India [gfr_2017:R161]. For other cases, the threshold is Rs. 50 lakhs [gfr_2017:R201].

rows.query: When may a limited tender enquiry be used for goods?
rows.answer: A limited tender enquiry (LTE) may be used for goods when the estimated value of the procurement is between Rs. 5 lakh to Rs. 50 lakhs [goods_manual_2024:4.8]. It is a restricted competition method where bids are invited from a preselected panel of registered suppliers for the subject matter of procurement [goods_manual_2024:4.8]. Additionally, LTE can be used for procurements above Rs. 50 lakhs in exceptional circumstances, such as urgent demand or when it is not in public interest to use advertised tender enquiry [gfr_2017:R162]. The process is designed to provide a simpler and quicker procurement method, especially for smaller-value procurements [goods_manual_2024:4.8].

rows.query: In what circumstances can goods be bought from a single source?
rows.answer: Goods can be bought from a single source under specific circumstances, such as when only a particular firm is the manufacturer of the required goods [gfr_2017:R166], or in cases of emergency where the required goods must be purchased from a specific source [gfr_2017:R166]. Additionally, single-source procurement may be justified for standardisation of machinery or spare parts to ensure compatibility with existing equipment, provided it is approved by the competent authority [gfr_2017:R166]. It may also be used for works that represent a natural continuation of previous work by the same firm, or when proprietary techniques are involved, and the selection is based on adequate justification [works_manual_2025:3.12]. For consultancy services, single-source selection is appropriate under exceptional circumstances like emergencies or when only one consultant has the necessary expertise [gfr_2017:R193].

rows.query: What amount of bid security (earnest money) should ordinarily be asked for?
rows.answer: The amount of bid security (earnest money) should ordinarily range between two percent to five percent of the estimated value of the goods, services, or works to be procured [gfr_2017:R170][ncs_manual_2025:6.1.1][works_manual_2025:5.1.1][goods_manual_2024:6.1.1][consultancy_manual_2025:6.1.1].

rows.query: Which bidders are exempt from furnishing bid security?
rows.answer: Based on the procurement rules, Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) as defined in the MSE Procurement Policy issued by the Department of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) and registered Startups as recognized by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) are exempt from furnishing bid security [gfr_2017:R170][consultancy_manual_2025:6.1.1]. Additionally, in appropriate cases, bidders may be exempt with the Competent Authority’s approval, especially in the case of indigenisation/development tenders, limited tenders, and procurements directly from the manufacturer or authorised agents [consultancy_manual_2025:6.1.1].

rows.query: What performance security should be taken from the successful bidder for a goods contract?
rows.answer: Performance security should be taken from the successful bidder for a goods contract, and it should be for an amount of three (3) to five (5) per cent of the value of the contract, as specified in the tender documents [goods_manual_2024:6.1.2]. The procuring entity may stipulate an upper ceiling for the performance security amount, depending on the tender value and market conditions [goods_manual_2024:6.1.2]. Additionally, the performance security should remain valid for a period of sixty (60) days beyond the completion of all contractual obligations [gfr_2017:R171].

rows.query: Can we split a Rs 12 lakh requirement into four smaller orders so that a lower authority can sanction each?
rows.answer: Based on the rules, splitting a Rs 12 lakh requirement into smaller orders to avoid higher authority sanction is not permissible [gfr_2017:R157]. Additionally, the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) rules prohibit splitting procurements into small quantities to avoid procurement through L-1 buying/bidding/reverse auction or higher authority sanction [gfr_2017:R149]. Therefore, the requirement cannot be split for this purpose.

rows.query: Does the Make in India order apply to a purchase estimated at Rs 4 lakh?
rows.answer: The Make in India order applies to purchases with an estimated value of up to Rs 200 Crore, as stated in Rule 161(iv)(b) of GFR, 2017 [works_manual_2025:1.11.2]. However, procurements with an estimated value less than Rs 5 lakhs are exempt from the order [ncs_manual_2025:1.10.2]. Since the purchase in question is estimated at Rs 4 lakh, which is below the Rs 5 lakh threshold, the Make in India order does not apply to it [ncs_manual_2025:1.10.2].

rows.query: What local content makes a supplier Class-I or Class-II under the Public Procurement (Make in India) order?
rows.answer: Under the Public Procurement (Make in India) Order, a supplier is categorized as a Class-I local supplier if the local content is a minimum of 50% [consultancy_manual_2025:1.10.2], and as a Class-II local supplier if the local content is a minimum of 20% [consultancy_manual_2025:1.10.2]. The Nodal Ministry/Department may prescribe a higher percentage for specific items [consultancy_manual_2025:1.10.2]. Local content is calculated as the value added in India, excluding net domestic indirect taxes and imported content [ppp_mii_order_2024:P2].

rows.query: What is the margin of purchase preference for Class-I local suppliers?
rows.answer: The margin of purchase preference for Class-I local suppliers is 20% [works_manual_2025:1.11.2]. This means that their quoted rates must fall within this margin to be eligible for purchase preference [works_manual_2025:1.11.2]. The preference is given over Class-II local suppliers and non-local suppliers, provided they meet the prescribed criteria for award of contract [works_manual_2025:1.11.2].

rows.query: Under GeM's terms, how soon must the buyer pay the seller for goods delivered?
rows.answer: Under GeM's terms, the buyer must pay the seller for goods delivered within ten (10) days of the issue of the consignee receipt-cum-acceptance certificate (CRAC) and online submission of bills, unless otherwise specified in STC / ATC [gem_gtc_4_0:C12]. For services, the payment is made within ten (10) days of the issue of the Service Delivery Acceptance Certificate (SDAC) and online submission of bills, unless otherwise specified in STC / ATC [gem_gtc_4_0:C12]. The payment terms are outlined in the GeM General Terms and Conditions (GTC) [gem_gtc_4_0:C12].

rows.query: What liquidated damages apply on GeM if the seller delivers late?
rows.answer: The liquidated damages for late delivery on GeM are calculated at 0.5% of the contract value of the delayed quantity per week or part of the week, up to a maximum of 5% of the total contract value, unless the delay is due to Force Majeure or other exceptions [gem_gtc_4_0:C15]. In case of inordinate delay, the maximum deduction can be increased to 10% of the total contract value [gem_gtc_4_0:C15]. The quantum of liquidated damages is also subject to the terms of any variations in the contract [ncs_manual_2025:9.4.7].

rows.query: How does the GeM Incident Management policy classify deviations by severity?
rows.answer:
The GeM Incident Management policy classifies deviations into four severity levels: Mild, Serious, Severe, and Grave [gem_incident_management_policy:2.1]. 

- **Mild Deviation**: These are deviations that have an impact on the functioning of other stakeholders [gem_incident_management_policy:2.1].
- **Serious Deviation**: These are deviations that have the potential to adversely impact the market ecosystem [gem_incident_management_policy:2.1].
- **Severe Deviation**: These are deviations that adversely affect the procurement process or cases of breach of contract [gem_incident_management_policy:2.1].
- **Grave Deviation**: These are deviations that adversely impact the reputation/credibility of the GeM and have the potential to significantly impact the market ecosystem of the GeM platform [gem_incident_management_policy:2.1].

The table at Annexure 1 depicts the deviations and their categorization [gem_incident_management_policy:2.1].

rows.query: Up to what value can the Secretary of a Department sanction expenditure on open or limited tender contracts under the DFPR?
rows.answer:
The maximum value threshold under the DFPR for expenditures that the Secretary of a Department can sanction on open or limited tender contracts is rupees one hundred crores [dfpr_2024:R11]. This threshold is specified in sub-rule (2) of Rule 11 of the DFPR. For contracts exceeding this value, the approval of the Minister in charge of the Department is required [dfpr_2024:R11]. 

The relevant regulations are found in Rule 11 of the DFPR, which outlines the powers of the Secretary of the Department concerning procurement [dfpr_2024:R11]. Additionally, the NCS Manual and Consultancy Manual also reference the DFPR and the delegation of financial powers [ncs_manual_2025:1.5][consultancy_manual_2025:1.5]. 

It is important to note that the Secretary may, with the concurrence of the DoE, re-delegate these powers to an Administrator or Head of the Department, but such delegation cannot exceed the limits specified in the DFPR [dfpr_2024:R11].

rows.query: Can a bidder from a country that shares a land border with India bid in our procurement?
rows.answer: A bidder from a country that shares a land border with India is eligible to bid in procurement processes only if they are registered with the Competent Authority [gem_gtc_4_0:C26]. This requirement applies to all procurements issued or published after 01.04.2023 [goods_manual_2024:1.11.4]. Additionally, if a bidder has a Specified Transfer of Technology (ToT) arrangement with an entity from such a country, they must also be registered with the Competent Authority [goods_manual_2024:1.11.4]. There are exceptions, such as procurements involving spare parts or raw materials from these countries, which are exempt from registration [goods_manual_2024:1.11.4].
